      Philosophy
      

      
      
        
      The arrangement
      
        
      A small model reads the question. An engine checks what the model wrote and does the calculation. Before either of them existed, a person wrote the rules. The three have separate jobs and none covers for another. The model may be wrong about English. It never does any arithmetic, so it cannot be wrong about that. The engine has no opinion about English. Its only input is a program, and it takes the program literally.
      

      
      
        
      The rules come first
      
        
      The ontology is the rulebook. It has 13 strands, from stories and fractions to trigonometry and calculus. Beneath them sit 290 problem types, the leaves. Each leaf names the relations and commands it needs, and there are 54 relations and 73 commands in all. Someone had to decide that “profit percent” is a thing before a model could be asked to find one. The model learns to read into that list. It cannot extend it.
      

      
      
        
      A closed language
      
        
      The model may only write programs in Rechen-Lisp, a closed language with exactly those relations and commands. A word outside the list is a syntax error. Numbers are held to the same standard: every number in the program must appear in the question. This is grounding. The model cannot invent a 17 to make a total come out. Fractions stay exact, so one third remains one third and no decimal rounds it away.
      

      
      
        
      Why it refuses
      
        
      When a check fails, the engine names the stage and stops: unknown form, ungrounded number, poor fit, no solution. A refusal costs the user a rephrasing. A wrong answer costs more, because it looks like a right one. So the page prefers silence to a guess. The program stays on screen beside every answer, so a person can read it, see what was understood, and fix the line that is wrong.
      

      
      
        
      What it still gets wrong
      
        
      On 150 held-back problems the large model is right on 90.0%. On a blind multi-step set of 200 it is right on 82.0%. About one answer in ten on the held-back set is confidently wrong. The cause is a consistent misreading: the program uses the question’s own numbers, passes every check and answers a different question. Two experiments went at this. One added more multi-step data. One made the model list every number it uses. Neither moved the numbers.
      

      
      
        
      Who edits it
      
        
      Humans improve this system by editing the ontology. They do not improve it by training. When a question fails, a person finds the missing problem type, the relation with the wrong roles or the check that was too loose, and changes the rulebook. A failure then points to a line of the rulebook, and a line can be argued over, tested and reverted. Weights cannot be.
      

      
      
        
      The measurements and the full argument are in the Paper section and in the PDF.

      The Model Only Reads: Ontology-Bound Parsing with a Fail-Closed Exact Engine for School Mathematics
      

      11 November 2026
      

      Abstract
      

      A 135-million-parameter language model that only translates, paired with an exact engine that only calculates, answers 90.0% of 150 held-back school mathematics problems correctly in a web browser. It gives a wrong answer on 8.7% and refuses 1.3%. On a harder blind set of 200 problems, 61% of them multi-step, it answers 82.0% correctly.
      

      We call the method ontology-bound parsing. A closed ontology of school mathematics (13 strands, 290 problem types, 54 relations and 73 commands) defines a small Lisp, Rechen-Lisp. The model reads a question and writes a program in it. A deterministic JavaScript engine checks that every number in the program comes from the question, solves the program in exact rational arithmetic, and writes the worked solution in text and LaTeX. When a check fails, the engine refuses to answer.
      

      We compare a model trained from scratch (11.5M parameters, 11.7 MB) with fine-tuned SmolLM2-135M, SmolLM2-360M and Qwen2.5-0.5B. Pretraining buys robustness to unfamiliar wording; model size beyond 135M buys nothing measurable. Hand-written training pairs are worth about as much as pretraining. The remaining errors are mostly dropped or duplicated steps in multi-step problems, and neither a targeted round of multi-step training data nor forcing the model to account for every quantity measurably reduced them.
      

      1 Introduction
      

      School mathematics needs two skills that small language models possess unequally. Reading a problem is a language task, which they do well. Calculating is an exactness task, which they do poorly: a model that can explain long division will still write 7 × 8 = 54.
      

      Large models hide the gap with scale. A model meant to run in a browser tab, offline, on a pupil's laptop cannot. The usual remedy is to let the model write code and run it. That removes arithmetic slips, but free-form code can express any misreading, and nothing checks the code against the question.
      

      We take the remedy one step further and close the language. The model may only choose from a fixed ontology of school-mathematics relations and fill their roles with numbers copied from the question. This has three consequences.
      

      • The model never calculates. The engine does all arithmetic and algebra exactly.
      • The engine can audit the program. A closed language makes it possible to check that each number is in the question and that the question's numbers are used.
      • Every relation is a teachable step. The engine inverts a relation for whichever role is unknown and narrates that inversion, so the worked solution follows the schema a teacher would name.
      

      Contributions
      

      1. Rechen-Lisp, a schema-based intermediate language for school mathematics from early arithmetic to first calculus, with an exact engine that explains its work and fails closed.
      2. A corpus method: programmatic generators organised by strand, plus hand-written pairs in many voices, plus hand-written test sets kept apart from both.
      3. A controlled comparison of a from-scratch 11.5M model with three fine-tuned pretrained models, including paired significance tests and an expert-program ceiling.
      4. A dependency-free browser runtime for the 135M model: int8 weights, a pruned tokenizer, 115.7 MB, about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds per answer.
      5. An error analysis that locates what remains: composition across steps, not vocabulary and not arithmetic.
      

      A note on the name
      

      The project began as a sibling of Plakatgeist, whose transformer weights are written by hand with no training. That method is weight-space programming. The model here is trained by gradient descent, so the term does not apply. What the two share is the idea that the model's whole output space is a small formal language with a checker behind it. "Ontology-bound parsing" names that idea directly; we use "reader" for the model and "reckoner" for the engine.
      

      2 Approach
      

      A question passes through one learned stage and four deterministic ones. Only the learned stage can be wrong silently; each deterministic stage can refuse.
      


      A refusal sends the page to the model's next candidate program; if none passes, the pupil is told the problem could not be read.
      

      1. Normalise. Unicode superscripts, currency signs, thousands separators and multiplication signs are mapped to one spelling. The same rules run in training and in the page, checked for parity.
      2. Read. The model continues the prompt question ⏎ => with one Rechen-Lisp program. Decoding is greedy.
      3. Check. The engine parses the program against the grammar: known relation, known roles, well-formed values.
      4. Ground. Every number in the program must be traceable to the question. A separate fit report measures the reverse: how much of the question the program used.
      5. Solve and explain. The engine solves the relations in dependency order with exact rationals and emits titled steps, each with text and LaTeX, then the answer.
      

      The fail-closed contract
      

      The engine refuses on an unknown form, a missing role, an ungrounded number, a contradictory or unsolvable system, or a fit report at its strongest mismatch level. In every evaluation run that level contained no correct answer, so refusing it costs nothing.
      

      When the first program is refused, the page tries the model's beam-search alternatives in order and labels any accepted answer a second attempt. If none is accepted, the page says it could not read the problem. Section 7 shows that this fallback adds little.
      

      The contract does not catch a consistent misreading. A program that uses the question's numbers in a plausible but wrong relation is accepted. That is the residual error this paper measures.
      

      3 Ontology and Rechen-Lisp
      

      The ontology was written before any code or data, and everything else is derived from it. It has 13 strands and 290 leaves; a leaf is one problem type a textbook would give its own exercise set.
      

      StrandScope
      storyArithmetic situations in words: change, combine, compare, equal groups, multi-step
      numNumber sense and operations without a story: place value, factors, powers, number words
      fdpFractions, decimals, percent
      ratioRatio, rate, proportion, motion
      moneyProfit and loss, discount, interest, wages, tax
      measureUnits, conversion, time
      geoGeometry and mensuration
      algExpressions, equations, systems, quadratics, factorisation
      coordCoordinate geometry and functions
      countSequences, counting, probability
      statStatistics and data
      trigTrigonometry
      calcDifferentiation and integration
      

      Relations
      

      A relation is a named schema with roles. One role holds ?, the asked unknown. The engine inverts the relation for whichever role that is, so a single schema covers every "which quantity is missing" variant of a problem type.
      

      (problem (kind money.trade)
  (trade (cost 800 rupees) (sell 920 rupees) (profit-percent ?)))
      

      The same trade relation with (cost ?) and a given profit percent is the reverse problem. The story relations follow the classic situation types of arithmetic word problems: change, combine, compare and groups.
      

      Chaining
      

      Multi-step problems are several relations linked by variables $a, $b, … Each variable is an unknown in one relation and a given in a later one, so a program is a small dependency graph.
      

      (problem (kind story.multi)
  (groups (what "friends") (count 4) (size 6) (total $a))
  (change (what "sweets") (start 48) (lose $a) (end $b))
  (groups (what "people") (count 2) (size ?) (total $b)))
      

      This is the program for "i had 48 sweets and gave my 4 friends 6 each. then i shared the rest with my sister equally. how many did i get".
      

      Commands
      

      Symbolic work uses commands over expressions. The formula is copied from the question as infix text; the model never rewrites it.
      

      (problem (kind alg.system)
  (unknown x "the larger number")
  (unknown y "the smaller number")
  (solve (system (= (+ x y) 20) (= (- x y) 4)) (for x y)))

(problem (kind calc.diff) (derive (expr "sqrt(4x + 1)") x))
      

      There are 54 relations and 73 commands. Commands include solve, factor, derive, integrate, evaluate and line, among others.
      

      Why schemas and not equations
      

      An equation-based target would ask the model to do the modelling step, turning "sold at a 10% gain" into 1.1c = 1980. A schema target asks only which relation the sentence states and which numbers fill it. That is a classification-and-copy task, which is what small models are good at, and it leaves the modelling knowledge in the engine where it is written once and tested.
      

      4 The engine
      

      The engine is plain JavaScript modules with no dependencies, so the same code runs in the browser and in headless tests. It has 263 unit tests, and its symbolic results were cross-checked against SymPy during development.
      

      Exact arithmetic
      

      Numbers are rationals over arbitrary-precision integers. Decimals in the question are read as exact fractions, and results are printed as integers, fractions or terminating decimals as the question's own style suggests. A small computer algebra system handles polynomials, equation solving, factorisation, differentiation and integration at school level.
      

      Grounding and fit
      

      Two checks compare the program with the question text.
      

      • Grounding runs from program to question. Each number in the program must appear in the question as a numeral, a number word, or a recognised implicit quantity such as a dozen. A hallucinated 5,000 where the question says 50,000 is refused.
      • Fit runs from question to program. It reports how many of the question's quantities the program left unused and grades the mismatch as clean, mild or strong. It was added after an early version accepted gibberish and programs that ignored half the question.
      

      Across all evaluation runs, no answer graded strong was correct. Answers graded mild were right about half the time for the 135M model on fresh problems (7 right, 4 wrong).
      

      Explanation as pedagogy
      

      Each relation carries its own narration for each possible unknown. Solving trade for the profit percent produces three steps: what is known, the subtraction that gives the profit, and the division by cost price with the reminder that profit percent is always taken on cost.
      

      \frac{920 - 800}{800} \times 100 = 15\%
      

      For a system of two equations the engine names the unknowns in the pupil's words, eliminates, back-substitutes, and checks the solution in both original equations. The steps are generated from the solving path, so the explanation and the answer cannot disagree.
      

      Three choices follow from treating the output as teaching material.
      

      1. The program is shown above the working, so a pupil or teacher can see how the question was read and correct it.
      2. A refusal is stated as a refusal, with the reason, and never replaced by a guess.
      3. Labels in the working are the question's own words (who, what), copied by the model, so the solution talks about oranges and buses, not x and y.
      

      5 Data
      

      Training data comes from two sources of very different size and character, and test data from a third that neither source may see.
      

      Strand generators
      

      A strand generator is a Python module that owns one strand of the ontology. For each leaf it draws numbers, names and objects, renders a question from many surface templates, and emits the matching program and answer. Shared lexicons hold 1,721 names and 1,302 nouns with compatibility classes, so that people buy mangoes and not squash rackets by the gross.
      

      Every generated triple is verified by running the program through the engine and comparing with the generator's independently computed answer. A 20,000-item random sample of the training corpus passed 20,000 of 20,000.
      

      Generators give volume and exact coverage of the ontology. Their weakness is voice: however many templates, they write like templates.
      

      Hand-written pairs
      

      We therefore wrote 3,600 question–program pairs by hand, in eight files by strand group. The brief asked for the voices real questions arrive in: NCERT, CBSE and ICSE textbooks and papers, GCSE, US Common Core, Singapore model-method, worksheets, a parent typing homework, a child typing without punctuation, and chat shorthand. Each answer was computed independently of the engine and each pair then verified through it.
      

      Of these, 300 were set aside before training as a held-out set, stratified by file. The other 3,300 were repeated 16 times in a stream with 600,000 generated examples, making them 8.1% of the training mix.
      

      Test sets
      

      SetSizeRole
      Fresh set 1300Hand-written by an author who saw neither generators nor training data. Used for steering during development.
      Authored held-out300Same authors and voices as the hand-written training pairs, never trained on. Harder: more multi-step problems.
      Fresh set 2150Written with set 1, held back, scored once at the end with nothing tuned afterwards.
      In-template validation2,000Generator output from an unseen seed. Measures fit to the templates only.
      

      A fifth set, fresh set 3, was written for the chain round of Section 7.6 after set 2 had been used: 200 problems by an author who saw only the ontology, not the language, engine or any data. It is deliberately harder, with 98 two-step and 25 three- or four-step problems, and was scored once.
      

      The expert ceiling
      

      Before trusting any model score we wrote an expert program by hand for every problem in fresh set 1 and ran those through the engine. The first pass solved 284 of 300; the 16 failures were gaps in the language and engine, not in any model. After fixing them the expert programs solve 300 of 300. The ceiling was tuned on set 1, so set 2 is the honest measure of language coverage as well as of the model.
      

      6 Models and browser runtime
      

      Four readers were trained on the same data and judged by the same engine.
      

      ModelParametersArchitectureTokenizerint8 file
      Scratch11.5M6 layers, width 384, 6 heads, GELU, RoPEOwn word-level, about 5,350 tokens, digits split11.7 MB
      SmolLM2-135M134.5M30 layers, width 576, grouped-query attention 9/3, SwiGLUByte-level BPE, 49,152137 MB full, 115.7 MB pruned
      SmolLM2-360M361.8M32 layers, width 960, grouped-query attention 15/5Sameabout 362 MB
      Qwen2.5-0.5B494.0M24 layers, width 896, grouped-query attention 14/2Byte-level BPE, 151,936about 494 MB
      

      Training
      

      The scratch model trains as a causal language model on question, separator, program, with a reduced loss weight of 0.1 on question tokens and mild input noise. It uses AdamW at learning rate 1e-3, batch 128, for 20,000 steps, which is 2.56 million examples or about 3.9 passes over the mix.
      

      The pretrained models are fine-tuned in full, with loss on program tokens only, at learning rate 1e-4 with 200 warm-up steps and cosine decay to 10%, batch 32. The first experiment ran 6,000 steps; the second ran 12,000 steps, which is 384,000 examples or about 0.59 of one pass. A sweep over 5e-5, 1e-4 and 2e-4 showed no difference outside noise.
      

      All training ran on one Apple M4 Max laptop. The scratch model took about 74 minutes and the 135M fine-tune 88 minutes.
      

      Browser runtime
      

      The 135M model runs in a Web Worker through a runtime written for this project, with no external library.
      

      • Weights stay as int8 with per-row scales in WebAssembly memory and are never expanded to floats. A relaxed-SIMD dot-product kernel gave about 2.5 times the speed of the plain SIMD one on Apple silicon.
      • Vocabulary pruning keeps only the tokens that occur in the training text and lexicons, closed under the merge rules that produce them, plus every single-byte token. Tokenisation is then identical to the full tokenizer on any text that uses only kept tokens, and falls back to a finer valid segmentation otherwise. This cut 49,152 tokens to 14,372.
      • Fidelity. The exported file writes the same program as the PyTorch model on 299 of 300 validation questions and 291 of 300 held-out authored questions. Of the 9 differences, 7 keep the same verdict and 2 change from wrong to right.
      • Speed. In headless Chrome an answer takes roughly 0.07 to 0.16 seconds at about 500 tokens per second. Peak memory was about 440 to 490 MB.
      

      Four-bit weights were tried and rejected: plain rounding to int4 on all matrices dropped correct answers on validation from 297 to 282 of 300 and was slower than int8.
      

      7 Experiments and results
      

      Every problem ends in one of three outcomes. Right: an answer was given and matches. Wrong: an answer was given and does not match. Refused: no answer was given. Wrong is the costly outcome, so it is reported beside right throughout. With 300 problems the 95% interval on one score is about ±4 points; paired tests on the same questions are tighter and are given where they matter.
      

      7.1 Does pretraining help, and how much model is needed?
      

      The first experiment used an earlier 300,000-example generated corpus with no hand-written pairs, and an engine snapshot on which expert programs solved 281 of 300.
      

      ModelRight %Wrong %Refused %In-template right %
      Scratch 11.5M76.319.34.397.2
      SmolLM2-135M85.312.72.098.5
      SmolLM2-360M87.39.73.099.3
      Qwen2.5-0.5B86.711.02.398.8
      

      Fresh set 1, greedy decoding. All four models are near-perfect on in-template questions, so that number says little. On fresh wording, pretraining adds 9 points and the three pretrained models are within noise of each other. The 360M model was flat from half-way through training.
      

      7.2 What do better data buy?
      

      The second experiment retrained the scratch and 135M models on the current generators (290 leaves) plus the hand-written pairs, judged with the current engine. Old predictions were re-judged on the same engine for comparison.
      


      Model and dataFresh set 1 (R / W / Ref %)Authored held-out (R / W / Ref %)In-template right %
      Scratch, old data77.3 / 18.3 / 4.3
      135M, old data86.3 / 11.7 / 2.0
      Scratch, new data88.0 / 10.7 / 1.363.3 / 30.3 / 6.397.5
      135M, new data93.0 / 5.0 / 2.081.3 / 15.0 / 3.799.15
      

      Paired exact McNemar tests on the same questions:
      

      • 135M against scratch on fresh set 1: 19 questions favour the 135M model and 4 the scratch model (p = 0.003).
      • 135M against scratch on the held-out set: 63 against 9 (p < 0.0001).
      • New data against old data: 39 against 7 for the scratch model, 23 against 3 for the 135M model.
      

      The new data helped the scratch model more (+10.7 points) than the pretrained one (+6.7). Scratch on new data edges the pretrained model on old data, so on this test the data were worth about as much as pretraining. The gap did not close, and on the harder held-out set it is 18 points.
      

      7.3 Where the gap is
      

      Strand (fresh set 1)nScratch old135M oldScratch new135M new
      story6036474753

      Counts of right answers. Algebra was the one strand pretraining did not help in the first experiment; new data fixed it for both models (32 to 38). Story problems remain the largest pool of errors.
      

      On the held-out set the gap concentrates in the hardest file, multi-step stories: the scratch model solves 5 of 42 and the 135M model 22 of 42. The scratch model saw each hand-written training pair about 63 times and still did not acquire the style; its vocabulary was not the cause, since out-of-vocabulary words are spelled out and never unknown.
      

      7.4 The shipped system
      

      The final numbers come from the exported int8 files running in the JavaScript runtime with the page's own answer policy. Fresh set 2 was scored once, after everything else was fixed.
      

      Weights fileSetPolicy (R / W / Ref %)Plain greedy (R / W / Ref %)
      135M, 115.7 MBFresh set 1 (300)93.3 / 6.0 / 0.793.0 / 5.0 / 2.0
      135M, 115.7 MBFresh set 2 (150)90.0 / 8.7 / 1.389.3 / 8.0 / 2.7
      Scratch, 11.7 MBFresh set 1 (300)89.3 / 10.7 / 0.088.0 / 10.7 / 1.3
      Scratch, 11.7 MBFresh set 2 (150)82.0 / 18.0 / 0.080.0 / 16.7 / 3.3
      

      Both models score 3 to 7 points lower on the untouched set than on the steering set, which is the size of the optimism that development on set 1 introduced.
      

      7.5 Decoding policy
      

      Beam search with engine veto does not beat greedy decoding for the pretrained models. In the first experiment it moved the 135M model from 85.3 / 12.7 / 2.0 to 84.3 / 15.0 / 0.7: refusals became wrong answers. In the shipped policy the beam is consulted only after a refusal. For the 135M model that rescued 2 right answers and added 4 wrong ones across both fresh sets.
      

      The practical reading is that a refusal from this engine is informative and should usually stand.
      

      7.6 A targeted chain round: no measurable effect
      

      Section 8 shows that most residual errors are multi-step. We tested the obvious remedy: more multi-step training data. The round added 59 generator leaves for two- to four-step problems, raising their share of generated data to 21.9%, and 1,500 pairs built from 115 hand-written multi-step frames filled with varied numbers and wording. Both models were retrained with otherwise identical settings.
      

      ModelFresh set 3 (200), newFresh set 3, beforePaired (new only / old only right)
      135M84.0 / 13.5 / 2.582.0 / 15.5 / 2.511 / 7, p = 0.48
      Scratch80.0 / 19.5 / 0.579.5 / 19.5 / 1.012 / 11, p = 1.0
      

      Right / wrong / refused in percent, page policy, scored once. The retrained models are 0.5 to 2 points ahead, far inside the ±5 point noise at this size. On the development sets the picture is the same: the 135M model moved from 93.3% to 94.7% on fresh set 1 and from 83.0% to 82.7% on the held-out set, and no paired test reached p < 0.2.
      

      The retrained 135M model did repair old multi-step failures, 5 of 13 on fresh set 1 and 10 of 30 on the held-out set, but on the held-out set it also broke 20 problems the previous model had right. The data moved errors around without removing them. The shipped weights were therefore left unchanged.
      

      Accuracy falls with the number of steps, for every model:
      

      Model (page policy)1 step (77)2 steps (98)3 to 4 steps (25)
      135M, shipped92.2%77.6%68%
      135M, chain round93.5%79.6%72%
      Scratch, shipped89.6%74.5%68%
      Scratch, chain round90.9%73.5%72%
      

      Of the shipped 135M model's 36 failures on fresh set 3, 34 are model misreadings, one is an answer-format mismatch (a ratio printed as 3:8 where the key lists 3 and 8), and one is a problem the language cannot express (the sum of the distinct prime factors of 210).
      

      7.7 Making the model account for every quantity: also no effect
      

      If more data does not help, perhaps structure does. We tested whether forcing the reader to account for every quantity in the question reduces multi-step errors. It does not. Numbers below are PyTorch greedy on the two development sets pooled (600 problems), then on fresh sets 2 and 3 pooled (350), which had each been scored once before and were not tuned on.
      

      How much can accounting see? For the chain-round 135M model, 21 of 58 failures leave a question quantity unused, and 24 of 58 show either an unused or an over-used quantity. The same signals flag 10% of right answers. About 40% of failures are visible to a quantity check at all; most misreadings use every number, wrongly.
      

      Engine-guided re-decoding, no retraining.
      

      MethodRightWrongRefusedFixedBroken
      Plain greedy5295813
      Page policy (beam after a refusal)53662270
      Forced continuation while quantities are unused5058213024
      Choose the accepted candidate that uses most quantities537621124
      

      Forcing the model to keep writing fixed nothing and broke 24 right answers: it invents a step for a number the question meant to be ignored. Choosing among candidates by coverage matches the existing page policy to within one answer.
      

      An accounting prefix, trained. The target was changed so the program first declares the quantities it will use and those it sets aside, for example (given 48 4 6) (spare 25), and a wrapper checks the declaration against the program and the question. A 135M model was retrained on the same data in this form with identical settings.
      

      Model and policyDevelopment (600)Fresh sets 2 and 3 (350)
      Chain-round model, plain greedy529 right, 58 wrong302 right
      Prefix model, prefix ignored531 right, 53 wrong303 right
      Prefix model, refuse on a failed check518 right, 39 wrong, 43 refused
      

      Paired, the prefix model wins 14 problems and loses 13 on the final sets. Used as a refusal rule the check removes about a quarter of wrong answers at the cost of 13 right ones, and it adds 28% more tokens per answer.
      

      The reason is visible in the failures. Of the prefix model's 17 development failures with fewer forms than the reference, none put the dropped quantity into spare, and 13 pass the accounting check. The model's plan agrees with its own misreading: it does not omit a step it knows about, it never registers the step.
      

      8 Error analysis
      

      Composition across steps is the main residual error, for both models and on every test set. Every failure on fresh set 1 and on the held-out set was classified against the expert program.
      

      Failure classScratch, fresh 1135M, fresh 1Scratch, held-out135M, held-out
      Multi-step chain wrong or incomplete16134830
      Wrong role or direction6273
      Number mis-copied531610
      Missing second ask or output option4293
      Wrong relation30247
      Formula mis-copied1010
      Unit or target1141
      Other0012
      Total362111056
      

      "Multi-step chain" is a broad class: any problem whose expert program has two or more forms and whose predicted program differs in structure.
      

      What pretraining fixed
      

      Pretraining mostly removed single-relation errors. Wrong relation fell from 3 to 0 on fresh set 1 and from 24 to 7 on the held-out set. Role and direction errors, such as gain for loss or base for part, fell by half or more.
      

      What it did not fix
      

      Seventeen fresh-set-1 problems and 47 held-out problems defeat both models. Typical unsolved cases across the sets:
      

      • A bus problem with two stops, where the second "3 got on" was dropped.
      • "i walk 3 km every day for 5 days then 2 km on sat and sun": both models miss that Saturday and Sunday are two days.
      • A speed asked in metres per minute and answered in metres per second.
      • A recurring decimal copied as 0.272727 where the language has a recurring form.
      • An age problem whose "in 2 years" clause was dropped.
      

      These are not vocabulary failures. They are failures to keep a count of clauses: how many events happened, how many quantities were asked, which intermediate result feeds which step.
      

      What the engine cannot catch
      

      On the untouched set, 14 of the 135M model's 15 failures were misreadings the engine accepted: a wrong quantity or operation, a duplicated or dropped clause, or count and total exchanged. One was a language limit: "which shop is cheaper" expects a name and the engine returns a number.
      

      The learning curve says where to spend effort. The 135M model went from 87.0% to 92.3% between 3,000 and 6,000 steps, then 92.7% and 93.0% at 9,000 and 12,000. More steps on the same data do nothing; the lever is more varied multi-step data.
      

      9 Limitations and threats to validity
      

      • Small test sets. The headline number rests on 150 problems, an interval of roughly ±5 points. Fresh set 2 has now been used once and cannot serve as an untouched set again.
      • Test sets written by language models. The fresh sets and the hand-written training pairs were authored by AI agents under briefs, not collected from classrooms. They are varied in voice but may share habits that real pupils' questions do not.
      • The held-out authored set shares authors with training data. It measures generalisation within those voices, not to new ones.
      • Scope is the ontology. A problem outside the 290 leaves is refused at best. Diagrams, tables in images, proofs, and open-ended questions are out of scope.
      • One answer format. Answers are matched as strings after normalisation. Equivalent forms the matcher does not know count as wrong.
      • Consistent misreadings pass. The fail-closed contract bounds one class of error and not the other; 8.7% of untouched problems still received a confident wrong answer.
      • English only, with Indian, British, American and Singaporean school conventions.
      • Runtime tested narrowly. Speed and memory were measured in headless Chrome on Apple silicon over a local connection. Safari, Firefox, other processors and a real 115 MB download were not tested.
      • No comparison with free-form code generation or a large model. We did not run a program-of-thought baseline on the same sets, so the benefit of closing the language is argued, not measured.
      

      10 Related work
      

      Twelve of the seventeen references were checked on their source pages. The other five (Bobrow, Riley et al., Kintsch and Greeno, Pólya, Ng and Lee) were confirmed from catalogue records and reference lists only.
      

      Semantic parsing of word problems. Translating word problems into equations goes back to Bobrow's STUDENT (1964). Later systems mapped problems to equation templates (Kushman et al., 2014) or expression trees (Wang et al., 2017, with Math23K; Xie and Sun, 2019). Ontology-bound parsing differs in its target: situation schemas with roles, not equations.
      

      Schema theory in mathematics education. The story relations follow the change, combine and compare categories of Riley, Greeno and Heller (1983) and the comprehension model of Kintsch and Greeno (1985). The multiplicative groups schema and the bar-model habits of Singapore mathematics (Ng and Lee, 2009) inform the worked steps. Pólya's (1945) four phases appear as known, plan, carry out and check.
      

      Program-aided reasoning. Program of Thoughts (Chen et al., 2023) and PAL (Gao et al., 2022) let a large model write Python that an interpreter runs. We keep the division of labour and replace the open language with a closed one that can be audited against the question.
      

      Benchmarks and robustness. MAWPS (Koncel-Kedziorski et al., 2016), SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021) and GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) are the standard word-problem sets. SVAMP showed that models exploit shallow cues; our split between in-template validation (97 to 99%) and fresh wording (76 to 93%) is the same phenomenon measured inside one project.
      

      Constrained and verified generation. Grammar-constrained decoding (Scholak et al., 2021; Geng et al., 2023) guarantees well-formed output. We do not constrain decoding; the engine rejects ill-formed or ungrounded programs after the fact, which also catches errors a grammar cannot express.
      

      Small models. SmolLM2 (Ben Allal et al., 2025) and Qwen2.5 (Qwen Team, 2024) are the pretrained bases. Weight-space programming, in which network weights are written directly with no optimiser, is the method of the sibling project Plakatgeist and is not used here.
      

      11 Conclusion and next steps
      

      A small model can be a dependable reader of school mathematics if it is asked only to read. With the calculation, the modelling knowledge and the explanation moved into an exact engine, a 135M model reaches 90% on untouched problems at 0.1 to 0.2 seconds per answer in a browser, and an 11.7 MB model reaches 82%.
      

      Three findings carry beyond this project.
      

      1. In-template accuracy is uninformative. Every model scored 97 to 99% on generator output while differing by up to 17 points on fresh wording.
      2. Pretraining and hand-written data are substitutes up to a point. Each was worth about 10 points on fresh problems; together they were worth 16.
      3. Capacity is not the constraint. Tripling and quadrupling the pretrained model changed nothing measurable. What is missing is exposure to varied compositions.
      

      What the chain round showed
      

      The chain round of Section 7.6 was the direct attempt on the residual, and it failed: more multi-step data of the same kind changed nothing measurable. Two readings are open. The added data may still be too template-like, since its 1,500 pairs come from 115 frames. Or the limit is comprehension. Section 7.7 tested the structural remedy, an explicit account of every quantity, and that failed too: the model's plan repeats its misreading. What both rounds leave standing is that the error is made while reading, before any program is written, and that neither more examples of the same kind nor bookkeeping after the fact reaches it.
      

      Open questions
      

      • Does a program-of-thought baseline with the same 135M model do worse than the closed language, and by how much?
      • Quantity accounting sees only about 40% of failures. Would a second, independent reading of the question (a verifier that restates the program in words and compares) catch the rest?
      • How much of the 115.7 MB can go with quantisation-aware methods without losing accuracy?

      B. More programs
      

      ; A truck is 100 km ahead of another. The one in front travels at 60 km/h and
; the one behind at 80 km/h. In how many hours will the second catch up?
(problem (kind ratio.motion)
  (compare (big 80 km/h) (small 60 km/h) (diff $s km/h))
  (motion (distance 100 km) (speed $s km/h) (time ? h)))

; A school has 450 students. 60% ride the bus. Each bus holds 45 students.
(problem (kind story.multi)
  (percent (what "students") (base 450) (rate 60) (part $a))
  (round-up (total $a) (size 45) (count ? buses)))

; Find the equation of the line through (6, -2) perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 8.
(problem (kind coord.line)
  (line (perpendicular (expr "3x + 4y = 8")) (through (point 6 -2))))

; eleven lakh twenty-two thousand three hundred, in figures
(problem (kind num.place)
  (number-words "eleven lakh twenty-two thousand three hundred"))
